healthContext: Asked by his sister how he looks, Charles draws himself plainly from winter quarters near Newtown: his messmates say he 'never was fatter,' round-shouldered as ever. The self-portrait affirms good health and adequate flesh despite deep snow and a notably thin Thanksgiving turkey ration.

Building breastworks inside the Nashville fortifications under Hood's advance, Alexander notes the heavy entrenchment labor 'comes pretty hard on me, but I will soon get inured to it again.' This is exertional strain from hard fatigue duty rather than illness, and he expects to reacclimate.

Convalescing at Chestnut Hill Hospital, Philadelphia, James reports a genuine wound (from the autumn 1864 Valley campaign) that has nearly healed; he can 'now walk around very well' and is restless to rejoin his regiment. A real wound classed serious even though downplayed and near full recovery, with a furlough denied because he is 'so near well.'

Alexander notes he has rigged a shanty and fireplace and is 'quite comfortable' against intense cold, and that on a wood-gathering foray beyond the pickets he 'was not fired at.' He reports no ailment of his own.

Frances (Mother) reports nothing of her own physical health. The letter's medical content concerns others: a hospitalized soldier she visited who 'is spitting blood' (possible pulmonary hemorrhage / consumption), and her acute dread that James, unheard from since Dec. 9, may have been sent to the front and killed or captured by guerrillas.

conditions.quote: to buy bread to keep life in me

healthContext: In a postscript Alexander recalls having had to sell his old watch 'to buy bread to keep life in me' — a retrospective, now-resolved glimpse of wartime privation when sick soldiers were not reliably fed. The debility tag is an inference from this hunger statement (no named illness); he is presently well and freshly paid. The letter's graphic amputation account (Chris Greene's leg severed with a pocket knife) concerns another man, not the author.

Charles affirms 'James & I are in good health.' He notes two ailments of others, not himself: James's new difficulty seeing after dark since reaching Savannah ('it troubles him to see at night, but he can see as well as usual in the day time') — classic nyctalopia / night blindness, a vitamin A deficiency common in camp on poor diet — and his mother's reported poor health.
